sections.h2: Where do Berrien County property owners deal with tax?
sections.html:
The Tax Commissioner is in Suite 105 on the ground floor of the Administration Building, 201 N. Davis Street, Nashville, Georgia 31639. Billing and payment questions go to (229) 686-7461, and the counter takes visitors on weekdays from eight until five. The commissioner bills and collects real property, personal property, mobile home, motor vehicle and timber tax.

Valuation is a different office. Berrien's Board of Tax Assessors sets values and takes homestead applications, and the Tax Commissioner's staff can point you to the assessors if you are unsure where to go.

  • Tax Commissioner: bills, receipts, payment help, liens.
  • Tax Assessor: values, returns, homestead and other exemptions.
  • Clerk of Superior Court: warranty deed copies at the courthouse deed room.

sections.h2: What should a Berrien County seller know about the county itself?
sections.html:
Berrien lies in south central Georgia, and a legislative act of February 25, 1856 carved it out of Coffee, Irwin and Lowndes. It spans 458 square miles, most of it rural, with the western side draining toward the Withlacoochee River and the eastern side toward the Alapaha. Irwin, Coffee, Atkinson, Lanier, Lowndes, Cook and Tift counties touch its borders. One school system, the Berrien County School District, covers every address.

The county lost an unusually high share of its young men in World War I, and a copper Doughboy memorial by E. M. Viquesney stands on the Nashville courthouse grounds. Headcount has swung: 19,286 in 2010, then 18,160, then an estimated 18,932 for 2025. Nearly three quarters of residents counted in 2020 lived outside urban areas, so most owners hold rural parcels rather than town lots.

The Census Bureau lists 8,328 housing units in 2025 and a 71.0 percent owner rate. Median household income is $52,876, and 18.0 percent of residents live in poverty.

sections.h2: When must Berrien County property tax be paid?
sections.html:
According to the tax office, houses, land and business equipment have been billed for a November 15 deadline each year since 2018. Mobile and manufactured homes keep an April 1 deadline, and vehicles follow the owner's birthday.

The same FAQ spells out lateness. A month of delay adds 1% interest, and a flat 10% penalty lands if the bill is still open three months after the deadline. Unpaid tax can turn into a FiFa lien at the Clerk of Superior Court, which the FAQ says is possible once a bill is 30 days overdue, and ultimately the commissioner may levy on the parcel.

Berrien's tax site runs on the GovtWindow platform, which lets owners search a parcel and pay online, and its help desk number is (877) 575-7233. Mobile and modular homes count as personal property in Georgia, so the owner files a return and gets a location permit, and the permit is issued only after that year's mobile home tax is paid in full. Timber tax is also billed by the commissioner, which matters for anyone selling acreage.

sections.h2: How does Berrien County calculate a tax bill?
sections.html:
The state taxes 40% of market value, and Berrien's county commissioners and school board each choose a millage every year. The tax office lays out the order of operations: take assessed value, subtract exemptions to reach net taxable value, then multiply by the mills. A mill raises one dollar on each $1,000 of that net figure.

Ask the commissioner for the millage on your parcel instead of guessing at it. Statements go to the owner. A lender that escrows for you needs a copy, so check that the servicer has the Berrien bill.

  • Returns: owners can name their own value any time in the first three months of the year.
  • Notice: the assessors send one when their value differs from the return.
  • Bill: the commissioner applies the adopted mills to net taxable value.

sections.h2: How is homestead claimed in Berrien County?
sections.html:
Both owning and occupying the house on New Year's Day are required. The application goes to the tax assessor's office and must be received before April 1. Filing is allowed year round, though a late application starts with the next tax year.

Approval carries over year to year at the same address. A move to another Berrien house means filing anew. Homeowners at 62 may apply for an added exemption, and business personal property can qualify for freeport relief. The dollar figures change with legislation, so the assessors are the source for current amounts.

sections.h2: What are my options if I dispute a Berrien County value?
sections.html:
The deadline is 45 days counted from the notice date. Take the appeal to the county Board of Equalization or an arbitrator, and if you remain dissatisfied, tell the Board of Tax Assessors in writing that you are continuing to superior court.

State guidance says a fair market value appeal sent by mail needs a postmark no later than day 45. Tax collected in error or illegally can be recovered when a written claim is made inside three years of payment.

sections.h2: What tax steps come before selling a Berrien County house?
sections.html:
Request the balance in writing from the commissioner before taking an offer, and confirm who is billed. The owner on January 1 gets the statement, so yours may still arrive after a fall closing. Whoever handles the closing can show how that year's tax is divided.

A FiFa on file is public and must be satisfied before the buyer gets a clean title. Farmhouses with old taxes, inherited deeds or deferred repairs can still sell as is, since the payoff is taken from the sale money. A cash buyer will ask for the same payoff number you hold. If the house is a rural parcel, also ask whether any timber tax or a mobile home account is attached to the same owner, since the commissioner bills those too, and settle each one before the deed is signed.

sections.h2: What do Census numbers say about Berrien County households?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau counts 7,045 households with an average of 2.58 people each, and about 92 percent of residents had not moved in the past year. Of adults 25 and older, 83.4 percent finished high school and 15.7 percent hold a bachelor's degree or more. About 55.3 percent of residents 16 and over are in the labor force, and the typical commute is 24.6 minutes.

The county counts 1,211 veterans, 253 employer businesses and 2,904 paid jobs in 2023, and 115 building permits were issued in 2025. Persons without health insurance under 65 stand at 15.7 percent, and 13.6 percent of residents under 65 report a disability. Retail sales were about $133 million in 2022, or $7,303 per resident. For context on pricing, the Census median owner-occupied value is $131,600 and median gross rent is $782 a month.

faqs.q: When does Berrien County want its property tax?
faqs.a: November 15 each year covers real estate and business personal property, on a schedule used since 2018. Mobile homes fall due April 1.

faqs.q: What does overdue Berrien County tax cost?
faqs.a: Interest is 1% a month from the due date, and a 10% penalty follows if 90 days pass without payment.

faqs.q: Where is the Berrien County tax office?
faqs.a: At 201 N. Davis Street, Suite 105, Nashville, inside the Administration Building, with phone (229) 686-7461 and weekday hours from 8 to 5.

faqs.q: How fast must a Berrien County assessment appeal be filed?
faqs.a: Inside 45 days from the date printed on the assessment notice. The appeal goes to the Board of Equalization or an arbitrator.

faqs.q: Does the Berrien tax bill go to my lender?
faqs.a: No. The commissioner mails statements to homeowners only. If your lender escrows, forward the bill or confirm the servicer is paying it.
